主要内容: Spark Therapeutics' Luxturna, the first gene therapy approved in the U.S., is priced at $850,000 for a one-time treatment, or $425,000 per eye for a rare inherited retinal disease. The therapy, approved by the FDA in December 2017, targets a condition that can lead to blindness, affecting between 1,000 and 2,000 people in the U.S. Luxturna works by delivering a healthy copy of the RPE65 gene to restore vision. Clinical trials showed significant improvement in patients' ability to navigate obstacle courses in low light after a year. Spark also introduced payment and access programs, including outcomes-based pricing, where payments are tied to the therapy's effectiveness. The company aims to ensure access for patients by offering financial support and logistics for travel. Luxturna will be available at half a dozen treatment centers in the U.S. this year. Spark's CEO, Jeff Marrazzo, emphasized the importance of affordability and long-term durability of the therapy. Similar models are being used by other companies, such as Novartis with Kymriah, which offers refunds if the treatment is ineffective. Spark has partnered with Express Scripts to offer insurers a direct purchasing option for Luxturna, avoiding the 'buy and bill' model. This initiative aims to reduce financial risks for treatment centers and lower markup costs for insurers. Express Scripts, as a pharmacy benefit manager, will negotiate drug prices and reimbursement on behalf of insurers and employers. Spark is also exploring staggered payment options for expensive one-time treatments, though challenges include government price regulations and frequent insurance provider changes. The company is in discussions with the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to potentially waive some requirements, enabling installment payments and larger rebates based on treatment effectiveness. Miller from Express Scripts emphasized the need to innovate in drug payment models as more expensive treatments enter the market.
